title: Don't guess (Avot 1:16)
hookLine: Gamaliel: find a teacher, free yourself of doubt, don't tithe by guesswork
carry: someone else's share was in the pile

cards: Dinner with six friends, one check. Somebody says, let's just call it about forty each. Nobody pulls out a calculator.
Somewhere at the table, the person who only had soup is quietly paying for someone else's steak, and the one who had the steak is quietly relieved. Nobody meant any harm. It was just a guess.
Today's sage worried about exactly that kind of guess, only his table was a farmer's harvest, and the people who went short were the poor.

teach.b: The chain now reaches Rabban Gamaliel, called the Elder. Tradition says he was Hillel's grandson, and the Mishnah gives him the title Rabban, our master.

His saying: make for yourself a teacher, remove yourself from doubt, and don't tithe by estimate too often. That last line needs a picture. In the land of Israel, parts of a farmer's harvest weren't his to keep.

teach.h: A HEAP OF GRAIN, A TENTH.
teach.b: Some went to the priests, a tenth to the Levites, and in certain years a tenth to the poor. So a farmer stands in front of a heap of grain. He can measure it, or eyeball it and say, that's about a tenth.

teach.h: A GUESS GOES WRONG BOTH WAYS.
teach.b: The commentators point out that a guess goes wrong both ways. Too little, and he keeps what belonged to someone else. Too much, and what he set aside isn't a proper tithe.
Either way, he's living with doubt. Now the first two lines make sense. Make for yourself a teacher: Pirkei Avot already said this, back with Joshua ben Perachyah.
Some commentators say that one was about learning, and this one is about decisions: when you don't know, ask someone who does, instead of making it up.

teach.h: ASK A TEACHER, LEAVE THE DOUBT.
teach.b: And remove yourself from doubt: don't leave important things resting on a shrug. It's a small, practical saying that reaches a long way. Guessing feels easier than measuring.
But when other people's share is in the pile, the easy guess costs somebody something.

how: Observant Jews in the land of Israel still separate tithes (ma'aser) from produce, and when a question of Jewish law comes up, many ask a rabbi rather than decide by guesswork.

o: measure and ask, when others' share depends on it
trust your gut, since first instincts are best
never decide anything without total certainty

games.q: what's inside the saying — tap the pairs.
p: ask instead of making it up
eyeballing a tenth of the grain

s: a tithe was a portion of the harvest for others
for the priests, the Levites, and in some years the poor.
the commentators say a portion set aside by a high guess isn't a proper tithe either.
make yourself a teacher appears only once in Pirkei Avot
Joshua ben Perachyah says it too. some read Gamaliel's as about decisions.

games.q: you're a farmer in front of a heap of grain. a tenth of it isn't yours to keep. what do you do?
o: eyeball it. about a tenth is close enough.
set aside extra, just to be safe.
games.why: Gamaliel says don't tithe by estimate. a guess goes wrong in both directions, and someone else's share is in the pile.

practice: Count each breath, in and out as one, and really count instead of estimating: one, two, three. If you lose track, don't round up; go back to one. It's harder than it sounds, and that's the point: attention is a kind of measuring.

wordCard.voice: Don't guess. Rabban Gamaliel's rule: find a teacher, step out of doubt, and measure what belongs to others instead of eyeballing it.

orig.note: Mishnaic Hebrew: don't tithe by estimates too often.

carryVoice: Your line: someone else's share was in the pile. A tenth is a number, not a feeling. Day two hundred forty-six, done.
